11.16.26 - Teams

Andrew Alvidrez injury update after frightening final ride in Las Vegas

Austin Gamblers cowboy undergoes surgery following frightening wreck in Las Vegas, remaining in good spirits as he begins his recovery in Texas.

By Harper Lawson

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 9:43
Instaread

FORT WORTH, Texas – If there's one thing the bull riding world knows about Andrew “Primo” Alvidrez, it's that the man doesn't know how to quit.

Not when the bull has already won. Not when his body is hanging in a position most riders would have abandoned seconds earlier. And apparently, not even when the largest bone in his body is broken.

On Saturday night inside T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas, the 30-year-old Austin Gamblers cowboy gave the PBR world another reminder of just how much punishment he's willing to endure.

Matched with Mystified in the final frame of the Gamblers' first matchup of the Championship weekend against their in-state rivals, the Texas Rattlers, following a first-round bye Friday night, Alvidrez had drawn exactly the kind of bull his team had come to rely on him to face.

An eliminator.

The kind of animal that can make even the best bull riders in the world look ordinary. The kind that requires a cowboy willing to put everything on the line for eight seconds.

For Austin, that cowboy was Primo.

Alvidrez had spent much of the season embracing that responsibility, taking on some of the toughest bulls in the pen while finding his place within a Gamblers lineup loaded with world-class talent.

And Saturday was no different.

When the gate cracked, Alvidrez went to work.

But just 2.09 seconds later, the ride was over.

Alvidrez, notorious for keeping his riding hand shut until the last possible moment, found himself in another vulnerable position as he came off Mystified. When he hit the dirt, the impact fractured his femur, the longest and strongest bone in the human body.

Then things got worse.

With Alvidrez still moving beneath him, Mystified stepped on the cowboy's back, ripping his jersey as the crowd watched in horror.

For a moment, it appeared the wreck might have caused a devastating back injury.

Rather than lying motionless on the arena floor, Alvidrez began army-crawling across the dirt on his stomach.

With a broken femur.

As Alvidrez struggled to move, the PBR bullfighters worked quickly to clear Mystified from the arena, giving the PBR Sports Medicine Team a safe path to reach the injured cowboy.

Once at his side, medical personnel helped Alvidrez sit upright, an extraordinary sight considering the severity of his injury.

The crowd erupted.

Then came perhaps the most unbelievable part of the entire ordeal.

He walked out.

With the help of sports medicine personnel on either side of him, Alvidrez made his way off the arena floor, his injured left leg hovering above the ground as he relied on the support of those around him.

Behind the chutes, he was placed in a wheelchair and taken to sports medicine before being transported to a local hospital for further evaluation.

The diagnosis was a displaced femoral shaft fracture.

And in typical Primo fashion, his reaction to breaking one of the strongest bones in the human body was almost as remarkable as the injury itself.

Even the sports medicine personnel attending to him initially hadn't suspected a femur fracture, in part because of how little Alvidrez appeared to react to the pain.

But there was no walking this one off. No pun intended.

Alvidrez underwent surgery to repair the fracture, with surgeons inserting a metal rod through the hollow center of his femur to stabilize the bone and hold it in proper alignment while it heals.

The procedure, known as intramedullary nailing, is a common surgical treatment for femoral shaft fractures.

Think of it like putting rebar inside concrete.

The rod provides internal support, helping maintain the bone's length and alignment as the fracture heals. Locking screws help secure the hardware in place, allowing the bone to recover around it.

The technique actually has roots in World War II, when German surgeons used metal rods to repair broken femurs, including those of Allied prisoners of war. Before the procedure became widely adopted, patients often spent months in traction, a treatment that used weights and pulleys to keep broken bones aligned while they healed. That meant prolonged periods confined to a hospital bed, increasing the risk of painful bedsores, blood clots and potentially deadly pneumonia. The development of intramedullary nailing changed that, allowing patients to get back on their feet much sooner rather than spending months immobilized.

In Alvidrez's case, the fracture occurred in the upper portion of the femoral shaft and was displaced, meaning the broken ends of the bone had shifted out of alignment.

It was also a short oblique fracture, meaning the bone broke at an angle rather than straight across.

Now back home in Texas, Alvidrez is already up and moving around, or as he puts it, “just been limping along.”

But if anyone understands the work required to get back, it's the former powerlifter from Seminole, Texas.

And judging by his attitude just hours after surgery, he hasn't lost much of his fight.

When asked how he was doing following the procedure, Alvidrez's response was short, sweet and accompanied by two emojis that probably surprised absolutely nobody who knows him.

“Broken femur but I got a rod in it now 💯💪🏽”

Only Primo.

While most people would still be trying to process the fact that they had just undergone surgery to repair the largest bone in their body, Alvidrez was already flexing.

In a social media post following the injury, the Austin cowboy thanked his team, the medical personnel who rushed to protect him, the surgeon who repaired his leg and the family members who came to support him.

“I truly see Jesus in all of you,” Alvidrez wrote. “The surgery was a success and should be back to riding in a matter of 6-8 months.”

He also shared that he was looking forward to spending time with his wife and preparing for the arrival of their first child.

For a cowboy whose faith has always been as much a part of his identity as his determination inside the arena, the message was fitting.

A successful surgery. A growing family. And another opportunity to trust the process.

Still, the injury came at a particularly difficult time for a Gamblers team that had been finding its rhythm heading into the biggest weekend of the year.

Austin head coach Michael Gaffney had watched Alvidrez grow increasingly comfortable in the lineup since joining the franchise during the 2026 season, following a brief stint with the Texas Rattlers.

For Gaffney, Primo wasn't simply another talented bull rider.

He was a competitor who brought a different kind of toughness to the team.

When Alvidrez first joined Austin, Gaffney described him as a worker who brought the tenacity, will and determination the Gamblers needed.

“He's a battler, and that's what I'm so excited about,” Gaffney said at the time.

That assessment became even more apparent as the season progressed.

Alvidrez began to find his place among his new teammates, embracing his role alongside fellow hard-nosed competitor Callum Miller. Gaffney affectionately referred to the pair as his “grit masters.”

And the results went beyond the numbers.

The coach had noticed a change in Alvidrez's demeanor, one that reflected a cowboy growing more comfortable with his surroundings.

“I think if you take a hand out, like Double A, if you said it didn’t [affect the team], it would be a fib,” Gaffney said of the impact of losing Alvidrez.

He pointed to the momentum Alvidrez had helped create over the final weeks of the season, particularly as he began finding his niche within the team.

For Gaffney, seeing Alvidrez enjoy being part of the Gamblers was just as encouraging as watching him ride.

For a team entering Championship Sunday with a chance to compete for its second PBR Teams title, losing a rider like Alvidrez meant more than simply filling an empty spot in the lineup.

His absence left Austin without a dependable rider who had taken on some of the toughest bulls all season. The Gamblers continued their championship pursuit Sunday, ultimately falling to the Arizona Ridge Riders in the semifinals before finishing third at the 2026 PBR Teams Championship.

And while Alvidrez couldn't be there to finish the fight on the dirt, his own battle was already underway.

Now back home in Texas, the cowboy has begun the long process of recovery.

And if his messages from home are any indication, he isn't interested in simply putting this experience behind him.

“Yes mam, there will be a comeback,” Alvidrez said. “Literally letting all these painful days engrave in my brain. I want to remember this BS when I'm back”

Spoken like a man who has never been particularly good at taking the easy way out.

Long before making a name for himself on the PBR's premier tour, Alvidrez was working in the oil fields of West Texas, cutting and grooving pipe to pay for his bull riding dreams.

That same work ethic, iron grip and stubborn determination have made him one of the toughest riders in the sport. And Saturday night in Las Vegas was no exception.

The road back won't be easy, but if there's one thing Primo has never been short on, it's faith and grit.

Recovery will require patience, rehabilitation and trust in the Big Man's plan.

For now, there will be crutches instead of bull ropes and physical therapy instead of practice pens.

But if there's one thing Alvidrez has proven, it's that a little pain has never been enough to stop him from army-crawling forward.

PBR wishes Alvidrez a full and successful recovery as he begins his journey back to the dirt.

Strictly Necessary Cookies

Always Active

These cookies are necessary for the website to function and cannot be switched off in our systems. These cookies do not store any personally identifiable information.

Analytics Cookies

These cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance of our site. They help us to know which pages are the most and least popular and see how visitors move around the site.    All information these cookies collect is aggregated and therefore anonymous. If you do not allow these cookies we will not know when you have visited our site, and will not be able to monitor its performance.

Functional Cookies

These cookies enable the website to provide enhanced functionality and personalisation. They may be set by us or by third party providers whose services we have added to our pages.    If you do not allow these cookies then some or all of these services may not function properly.

Advertising Cookies

These cookies may be set through our site by our advertising partners. They may be used by those companies to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant adverts on other sites.    They do not store directly personal information, but are based on uniquely identifying your browser and internet device. If you do not allow these cookies, you will experience less targeted advertising.

Social Media Cookies

These cookies are set by a range of social media services that we have added to the site to enable you to share our content with your friends and networks. They are capable of tracking your browser across other sites and building up a profile of your interests. This may impact the content and messages you see on other websites you visit.    If you do not allow these cookies you may not be able to use or see these sharing tools.
